technique.how: With the patient supine or seated and the arm relaxed, place a dry, ungloved finger or the back of the hand into the axillary vault and feel for moisture. Check both axillae; the sign is positive when neither axilla is moist to touch.
technique.prerequisites: Axilla not recently washed, dried or covered by antiperspirant; room not cold. Compare with the patient's baseline sweating if known.
technique.contraindications: None; avoid if axillary skin is broken or infected.

interpretation.positive_finding: Both axillae dry to touch, supporting hypovolemia in a patient with vomiting, diarrhea or poor oral intake (LR+ about 2.8).
interpretation.negative_finding: Moist axillae argue only weakly against hypovolemia; the negative LR was not reported in the RCE abstract and the sign has low sensitivity.
interpretation.pitfalls: Anticholinergic drugs, autonomic neuropathy, cold environments and antiperspirants dry the axilla without hypovolemia; sweating from fever or anxiety can mask true volume depletion.
interpretation.changes_what: A dry axilla modestly raises the probability of hypovolemia and supports checking electrolytes, BUN/creatinine and giving a fluid trial; a moist axilla does not exclude it.

estimates.target_condition: Hypovolemia (dehydration) in adults with vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
estimates.population: Adults (largely elderly) presenting with suspected hypovolemia due to vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
estimates.reference_standard: Laboratory/clinical criteria for hypovolemia used by the included primary studies (e.g. serum osmolality, urea/creatinine); details not visible in abstract
estimates.quote: the presence of a dry axilla supports the diagnosis of hypovolemia (positive likelihood ratio, 2.8; 95% CI, 1.4-5.4)

sources.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
Eaton D, Bannister P, Mulley GP, Connolly MJ. Axillary sweating in clinical assessment of dehydration in ill elderly patients. BMJ. 1994;308(6939):1271-1272.
Levitt MA, Lopez B, Lieberman ME, Sutton M. Evaluation of the tilt test in an adult emergency medicine population. Ann Emerg Med. 1992;21(6):713-718.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use to exclude hemorrhage or shock; the RCE data apply to vomiting/diarrhea/poor intake, not blood loss.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Hypotension, severe postural dizziness or a postural pulse rise of 30/min or more indicates significant volume loss regardless of axillary moisture.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reproducibility not reported in the RCE abstract; the sign is a subjective tactile judgment.

extraction_notes: LR+ 2.8 (1.4-5.4) taken from the JAMA RCE abstract (PMID 10086438). Sensitivity, specificity and LR- for dry axilla are in the RCE tables, which are not accessible (JAMA not OA), so they are left null. Primary studies Eaton 1994 BMJ (PMID 8205020; PMC2540218 is abstract-only, no body text) and Levitt 1992 (PMID 1590613; abstract reports only that lack of axillary sweat was associated with greater dehydration, P=.026) are cited as sources without numeric estimates. Ids beyond the seeded mapping were not added.
